strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration of L2 reconstruction loss limitations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across Atari 100k (26 games), Hollow Knight (7 bosses), and Meta-world (4 tasks)
Extensive ablation studies examining input modalities, annotation count, policy architecture, and segmentation robustness
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations with concrete failure examples in appendices
Strong empirical analysis including reconstruction validation (Section 5.1), vector vs. mask comparison (Section 5.2), and robustness to detection errors
Practical integration of foundation vision models with MBRL demonstrating successful system design
weaknesses: Manual annotation requirement (6-12 masks per environment) severely limits generality; no automatic object discovery provided; contradicts sample-efficiency goals by not accounting for annotation cost
Limited technical novelty—primarily engineering effort combining existing Cutie and STORM components with straightforward concatenation; minimal architectural contributions

Inconsistent experimental results on Atari: improves only 18/26 games (69%); large negative results on 8 games (BattleZone: 13540→4590, Assault: 1526→1270); modest HNS improvement (~20%) with annotation overhead
Table 2 reveals method only benefits when 'all key information representable as objects'—highly selective and post-hoc applicability characterization

Hollow Knight evaluation concerns: non-standardized setup, only STORM baseline comparison (authors acknowledge difficulty comparing with prior work), custom non-standard reward shaping, only 3 random seeds, 0% win rate on Pure Vessel even at 400k samples
No principled method to predict a priori whether a task benefits from object-centric approach; generalization to unseen environments not demonstrated
Computational cost of Cutie not analyzed; cost-benefit analysis of annotation effort missing
Background representation problem acknowledged but unsolved; proposed solutions (Lin et al. 2020) fail for contactless interactions
Limited comparison with prior object-centric RL work; FOCUS comparison restricted to vector vs. mask representations only; no evaluation of end-to-end slot attention or SAVi variants at this scale

strengths: Clear problem motivation with concrete examples (Hollow Knight reconstruction) showing limitations of L2 loss in visually complex environments
Thoughtful selection and justification of Cutie over alternatives (compact representations, temporal consistency, few-shot learning capability)
Comprehensive experimental scope across Atari 100k and Hollow Knight with useful task categorization (Table 2) revealing when method applies
Thorough ablation studies and analysis including object representation completeness, vector vs. mask trade-offs, and annotation quantity sensitivity
Honest discussion of fundamental limitations (duplicate tracking failures, background representation issues) rather than overselling
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed loss functions, hyperparameters, environment configuration, and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward combination of existing STORM and Cutie methods with standard spatial-temporal transformer architecture—primarily an engineering contribution rather than methodological advance
Critical practical limitation: requires 6-12 manual annotations per environment with no systematic analysis of annotation cost, time required, or annotation cost vs. performance gain trade-off

Inconsistent Atari results: outperforms STORM on only 18/26 tasks (69%); median HNS improvement negligible (43.8% vs 42.5%); performance substantially degrades on non-object-representable games (124% vs 130% in Table 2)
Substantial underperformance on several Atari tasks: Assault (20% worse), Hero (44% worse), PrivateEye (15% worse)—method actively hurts performance on ~40% of benchmarks

Weak Hollow Knight evaluation: only compared against STORM baseline, not other methods; Hollow Knight not established benchmark; methodological confounds (different reward shaping Section D.4, different action space formulation, STORM* configured differently); only 3 seeds vs 5 for Atari
Missing critical baseline: no direct comparison with FOCUS (Ferraro et al., 2023), the most similar work using segmentation masks with DreamerV2, despite claiming vector representations are superior

Heavy dependency on Cutie segmentation quality: documented failure modes (duplicate tracking, out-of-domain limitations); entire approach outdated if better segmentation emerges; Appendix K shows performance degrades with detection errors but dependency not systematically analyzed

Experimental confounds: unclear if STORM baseline received equal hyperparameter tuning; 'lightweight STORM* configuration' for Hollow Knight (footnote Table 1) is a confound; novel reward shaping (life-loss as termination) makes attribution ambiguous
Statistical significance unclear: Atari shows standard deviations in figures but no formal hypothesis tests; some differences appear within noise; Hollow Knight uses only 3 seeds

Limited evaluation scope: all experiments on games; Meta-world experiments (Appendix J) only 4 tasks with minimal discussion; no real-world or robotics experiments despite practical value claims; generalization to non-game domains unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies limitation of reconstruction-based MBRL in visually complex environments where L2 loss misses small decision-critical objects
Thoughtful system design with justified selection of Cutie over alternatives and principled integration of object features with raw observations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper ablations, multiple domains (Atari and Hollow Knight), and excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices
Honest analysis of applicability with clear categorization of when method helps (object-centric games: 142.8% vs 116.5%) vs. doesn't (non-object games: 124% vs 130%)
Solid empirical results in target domains: 18/26 Atari games improved, significant gains on Hollow Knight bosses, reconstruction analysis validates STORM's failure modes
Practical approach leveraging frozen pre-trained models, eliminating need for fine-tuning and enabling out-of-domain generalization
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing components (Cutie, STORM, standard spatial-temporal transformer) without novel loss functions, architectures, or learning algorithms
Mixed and environment-specific results: only 18/26 (69%) Atari games improved, worse performance on non-object-centric games (124% vs 130% HNS), median HNS lower than baseline (43.8% vs 42.5%)

Manual annotation requirement (6-12 masks per environment) is practical limitation without rigorous cost-benefit analysis; justification ('informing agents of rules') is philosophically debatable and limits generality
Hollow Knight benchmark not established: only compared against STORM baseline, acknowledged unfair comparison with Yang (2023), custom environment setup limits reproducibility

Unresolved fundamental limitations: Cutie struggles with duplicate objects with no principled solution; background information (walls, boundaries) cannot be represented as objects, reintroducing L2 reconstruction problems; heavy dependence on frozen segmentation model
Limited scope of evaluation: only 26 Atari games, minimal Meta-world experiments (4 tasks), no real-world domains, no direct comparison with FOCUS (most similar prior work)
Missing computational analysis: no discussion of wall-clock time, memory overhead, or FLOPs compared to baselines despite higher resolution inputs required for Cutie
Statistical concerns: 5 seeds (Atari) and 3 seeds (Hollow Knight) with no formal significance testing; some improvements within confidence intervals

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear illustration of pixel reconstruction biases in MBRL
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two visually diverse domains with extensive ablations
Practical approach leveraging frozen pretrained segmentation models
Strong results on object-detectable Atari games (186.2% vs 147.7% baseline) and improved convergence on Hollow Knight
Thorough documentation with detailed appendices, hyperparameters, and implementation details
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing segmentation models (Cutie, SAM2) to STORM with straightforward architectural changes
Manual annotation requirement (6-12 frames per task) undermines sample-efficiency claims and scalability
Environment-dependent performance: achieves only 73.3% vs 72.0% on games where object detection fails, suggesting limited generality
Hollow Knight evaluation on non-standard, un-benchmarked domain with only STORM comparison makes it difficult to assess true competitiveness
Post-hoc partitioning of Atari games into 'Obj-detectable' vs 'Otherwise' raises methodological concerns about result interpretation
Weak analysis of FOCUS (closest related work) relegated to single table; no detailed investigation of why vector features outperform masks
No analysis of what world models actually learn differently with OC representations; limited interpretability and insight into mechanisms
Missing clean ablation isolating OC contribution from spatial-temporal architecture changes
Scalability concerns: requires manual specification of K objects, 50-70% computational overhead, unclear behavior with many objects
Robustness analysis (Section 5.2) uses artificial random zeroing rather than realistic segmentation failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem: pixel-level reconstruction loss biases toward backgrounds
Extensive experimental work with multiple ablations (backbones, segmentation methods, representations, robustness analysis)
Good analysis of when method works (obj-detectable games 186.2% vs otherwise 83.4%)
Honest about limitations (duplicated instances, geometric structures)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices (architecture, hyperparameters, annotations)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily concatenates pretrained segmentation with existing MBRL; largely incremental over FOCUS (Ferraro et al. 2023) which uses masks instead of vectors
Manual annotation requirement (6-12 frames) contradicts 'few-shot' claims and severely limits practical applicability
Weak Atari 100k results: OC-STORM (134.8% HNS mean) trails DIAMOND (145.9%) and Δ-IRIS (138.3%); no error bars, no significance tests on 5 seeds
Circular reasoning: post-hoc categorization of games as 'obj-detectable' makes method appear to work when segmentation already works; provides no value when segmentation fails
Hollow Knight is non-standard benchmark: mainly compares against STORM baseline; Appendix E.6 comparison with Yang (2023) uses different rewards/settings/configurations; only 3 seeds
Severe computational overhead: ~5× slower sampling (114→27 it/s), ~1.5× slower training (8.1→5.3 it/s) glossed over despite practical significance
Segmentation brittleness: complete external dependence; rapid degradation beyond ~25% detection failure (Section 5.2); handles neither duplicates nor geometric structures
No comparison with other object-centric RL methods or recent MBRL baselines; missing fair comparisons with methods using internal game states
Position information validation only on Boxing; masked pooling may lose spatial information in complex scenes
Overclaimed results: 'state-of-the-art sample efficiency' contradicted by DIAMOND; 'first to integrate' overstates existence of FOCUS

strengths: Clear problem formulation with strong motivation: pixel-level reconstruction ignores small task-critical objects, effectively illustrated in Figure 1
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse benchmarks (Atari 100k, Hollow Knight, Meta-world), multiple MBRL backbones, multiple segmentation methods, with well-designed ablations

Excellent analysis demonstrating practical insights: vector representations outperform masks due to resolution issues; feature completeness validated via reconstruction; robustness tested with realistic failure modes
Exceptional reproducibility: detailed architecture specifications, complete hyperparameters, implementation details, sample annotations, and extensive appendices enabling full replication
Honest discussion of limitations with supporting evidence (Appendix I): duplicated instance tracking and geometric structure representation challenges clearly identified
Practical contribution leveraging recent foundation models (SAM2, Cutie) with minimal annotation requirements (6-12 frames), making the approach viable for practitioners
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is primarily engineering—combining existing components (Cutie/SAM2 with STORM/DreamerV3) rather than introducing novel methods. The spatial-temporal architecture uses standard alternating attention blocks

Modest Atari 100k improvements: HNS median 43.8% marginally exceeds STORM (42.5%), and HNS mean (134.8%) trails DIAMOND (145.9%). Benefits highly environment-dependent (obj-detectable: 186.2% vs. otherwise: 83.4%)

Requires manual annotation per environment and manual specification of object count K, limiting applicability to novel domains. No ablation on sensitivity to incorrect K, and minimal guidance on selecting which objects to annotate

Hollow Knight not an established benchmark: custom environment wrapper, non-standard reward shaping, acknowledged lack of fair comparison with prior work (Yang 2023). Only 3 seeds, 7 bosses tested, limiting statistical confidence
Limited engagement with related object-centric RL work: only FOCUS compared; Nakano et al. (2024) and other supervised OC approaches not thoroughly compared, weakening positioning claims
Visual module still required for many environments despite object-centric framing, as geometric structures (walls, navigable spaces) are poorly represented by object features
Non-trivial computational overhead (55% training time increase: 3.67h→5.70h, plus 1500ms Cutie loading) insufficient discussion in main text
Object feature representation performance heavily dependent on foundation model details: Cutie (2,048-dim) vastly outperforms SAM2 (256-dim) without principled selection criteria
